name: Face yoga / face exercises

card.summary: Repeated facial-muscle movements promoted for toning and de-puffing the face; small studies exist but good evidence for appearance changes is limited.
card.aka: Facial exercises, facial yoga, facial gymnastics
card.note: Available trials are small, and studies on puffiness are mostly in surgical or TMD patients rather than healthy people.

quick.overview:
Face yoga refers to routines of facial muscle contractions, stretches and massage-like movements. It is marketed for anti-aging and, in looksmaxxing circles, for reducing puffiness and improving facial tone.

Published research is sparse. There is a 2014 systematic review of facial exercises for rejuvenation, a small 2025 pre-experimental study in 12 middle-aged women, and trials in other settings such as temporomandibular dysfunction and swelling after nose surgery.
quick.mechanism: Proponents propose that exercising facial muscles increases their tone and bulk and may help move fluid. Researchers have measured outcomes such as muscle tonus, stiffness and elasticity, but the proposed mechanisms for cosmetic changes remain under study.
quick.risks: Gentle facial exercise is not associated with major documented harms in the studies listed. Some people discussing the practice raise concern that repeated muscle contraction might deepen expression lines; no study cited here tested that.

lead: Face yoga, also called face exercises, facial gymnastics or facial fitness, is a set of routines involving repeated contraction, stretching or massage of facial muscles. It is promoted as a non-surgical, equipment-free way to look younger, tone the face, fill out or lift the cheeks and reduce puffiness.[1][2]

Unlike most other skeletal muscles, facial muscles attach to the skin, so when they contract they move the overlying skin; practitioners reason that changing the tone or size of muscles such as the zygomaticus, orbicularis or buccinator can change how the cheeks, brow, mouth and jawline look.[11] People follow named sequences of movements, often practised daily for several weeks and taught through books, apps, videos and social media. In looksmaxxing forums the practice is mentioned alongside fat loss, posture, lymphatic massage and gua sha as a soft-tissue approach to cheek fullness, puffiness and facial definition.[6][7]

Published research is small. A 2014 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal found nine reports, all positive but none controlled or randomized.[1] A 2018 JAMA Dermatology pilot study of 27 women aged 40 to 65 (16 completers) reported improved cheek fullness ratings and lower estimated age after 20 weeks, and a 2025 pre-experimental trial in 12 women measured changes in facial muscle tone, stiffness and elasticity.[8][2] Related trials have looked at face yoga in temporomandibular dysfunction and in swelling after nose surgery.[3][4]

angle.text: Practitioners use facial exercises to try to tone and lift the face and to reduce puffiness without procedures. The small studies measure muscle properties and cheek fullness ratings in middle-aged women.[2][8]

paras: Face yoga programs consist of named facial movements, often performed for a set number of repetitions over several weeks, and are distributed via books, apps and social media; specific routines vary from program to program.[2][8] The name borrows from yoga, but programs are modern facial-exercise systems rather than part of classical hatha yoga practice. The 2018 trial's program contained 32 facial exercises taught by a certified instructor.[8]

Exercise-style approaches differ from massage-based routines such as gua sha or lymphatic drainage, although many programs combine movement with massage and neck or posture work. Forum posters who discuss facial exercises tend to pair them with fat loss and posture, and some single out cheek, chin and jaw routines.[6]

sections.h: How people use it to improve their looks
paras: Practitioners aim at three looks: fuller, lifted cheeks, a firmer jaw and chin area, and a less puffy face. Middle-aged users emphasise anti-aging, which is the population studied in the main trials; younger users in looksmaxxing communities ask about cheek fullness, zygomaticus (smile-muscle) work and chin or jaw routines.[8][2][10]

The usual pattern in the studies is daily practice at first and then less frequent maintenance. The JAMA Dermatology program had two live 90-minute training sessions, 30 minutes a day at home for 8 weeks, and then practice every other day to week 20.[8] The 2025 trial used two supervised sessions and five home days per week for 8 weeks.[2]

Proponents describe two routes: building tone and bulk in muscles such as the zygomaticus, masseter or orbicularis, and releasing overactive muscles that they say contribute to lines or tension. The authors of the 2018 pilot proposed that improved fullness might result from exercise-induced muscle growth.[8]

The 2025 trial measured muscle properties with a handheld Myoton PRO device and reported that tonus and stiffness fell in some muscles (frontalis, corrugator supercilii, orbicularis oculi and oris) and rose in others (buccinator and digastric), while elasticity rose in all evaluated muscles; the authors concluded that effects depend on each muscle's structure and function.[2]

Forum users add a third idea: reducing water retention in the cheeks through muscle pump and lymph movement. One looksmax.org reply to a user with persistently full cheeks suggested that the appearance may reflect water retention rather than structure.[7]

Facial exercise for rejuvenation was being discussed in the medical literature as one of several non-medical alternatives to surgery, including facial acupuncture and acupressure, by the time of the 2014 systematic review.[1] The best-known controlled-style study, a 2018 pilot at Northwestern University, used a program from Happy Face Yoga, whose founder Gary Sikorski taught the sessions and is a coauthor; senior author Murad Alam disclosed consulting for companies unrelated to the work, and the study was funded by departmental research funds.[8]

The practice spread through books, apps and social media videos, and a 2025 paper describes face yoga as continuing to be popular as an anti-aging technique.[2] Looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a low-cost option for young people or those without access to procedures.[6]

A 2014 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal searched Medline, Web of Science, Science Direct, SciELO and LILACS and identified nine reports on facial exercises for rejuvenation. All nine reported positive outcomes, but none used a control group or randomization; they were single case reports, small case series or single-group pretest-posttest studies, and most assessments were subjective and unblinded. The authors concluded the evidence was insufficient to determine effectiveness and called for large randomized trials.[1]

A 2018 pilot study in JAMA Dermatology (NCT01689012) enrolled 27 women aged 40 to 65 with photodamage and mild to moderate facial atrophy; 16 completed 20 weeks of the program. Two blinded physicians rated photographs: upper cheek fullness improved (from 1.8 to 1.1), lower cheek fullness improved (1.6 to 0.9), and estimated age fell from 50.8 to 48.1 years; most other photoscale measures did not change significantly. The study had no control group and 11 participants did not finish. The authors wrote that the program may modestly improve the facial appearance of selected middle-aged women.[8]

A 2025 pre-experimental clinical trial in Medicina enrolled 12 women (mean age about 50) in eight weeks of intensive face yoga, measuring tonus, stiffness and elasticity with a Myoton PRO device; it reported the muscle-specific changes above and had no control group.[2]

A 2024 randomized controlled trial of 90 patients with temporomandibular dysfunction compared dry needling, face yoga and a control group over six weeks, reporting reduced pain and greater jaw movement in the dry needling and face yoga groups; this concerns a medical condition rather than appearance.[3] A 2026 prospective controlled study in the American Journal of Otolaryngology of 70 septorhinoplasty patients (43 face yoga, 27 control) used twice-daily exercises for 14 days and reported lower edema, bruising and discoloration scores on day 14 as rated by four blinded otolaryngologists.[4]

The trials above reported no serious adverse events in their abstracts; the postoperative study describes face yoga as safe, non-invasive and cost-free.[4] Some forum posters raise a different concern about related jaw exercises, saying muscle bulk can give a swollen rather than defined look.[9]

Posts on looksmax.org range from enthusiastic to dismissive. Threads ask whether specific videos are legitimate, which exercises target the zygomaticus muscles, and whether exercises help cheeks that look full despite low body fat; others treat the practice as a fallback for people who are young or cannot afford procedures, ranking surgery, appliances and fillers above it.[5][6][7][10]

A skeptical thread argues that facial aesthetics are determined primarily by bone, that exercise acts on soft tissue and that small facial muscles do not respond to hypertrophy training like other muscles.[9]

lore.intro: Face exercises are a frequent topic on looksmax.org, where some members try them for cheek, chin and jaw definition and others argue they cannot change bone structure.[5][6][7][9]

claims.claim: Chin and cheek exercises can produce visible change quickly.
claims.believers: The author of a thread titled as a 'copecels' guide said he was surprised by how quickly he saw changes from a chin exercise video, while ranking surgery, appliances and fillers above exercises.[6]
claims.experts: A 2014 review found positive results in nine reports but none controlled or randomized, and a 2018 pilot reported improved cheek fullness scores in 16 women.[1][8]

claims.claim: Facial exercises cannot remodel bone and only affect soft tissue.
claims.believers: A thread argues that facial aesthetics are determined mainly by bone, that exercise affects soft tissue and that facial muscles are small and not built for hypertrophy.[9]
claims.experts: The published exercise studies measure muscle properties, fullness ratings and estimated age rather than bone structure.[2][8]

claims.claim: Full cheeks at low body fat can be addressed with exercises or by fixing water retention.
claims.believers: A user with chubby cheeks at about 14 percent body fat asked whether exercises work; replies pointed to swallowing and tongue posture or to water retention.[7]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested exercises for cheek fullness at low body fat in men; the 2018 pilot enrolled women aged 40 to 65.[8]
A 2026 prospective study of 70 septorhinoplasty patients reported lower edema and bruising scores at day 14 with twice-daily exercises, a surgical rather than everyday context.[4]

claims.claim: Face yoga makes the face look younger.
claims.believers: Programs are marketed for anti-aging, and a 2025 paper describes face yoga as continuing to be popular for that purpose.[2]
claims.experts: In the 2018 pilot, blinded raters estimated participants at 48.1 years versus 50.8 at baseline, in a study with no control group and 11 of 27 dropouts; the 2014 review called evidence insufficient.[8][1]

claims.claim: Repeated facial contractions could deepen expression lines.
claims.believers: Some people discussing the practice raise this worry about repeatedly contracting the same muscles.
claims.experts: No study cited here tested whether face yoga deepens lines; the 2025 trial reported lower tonus and stiffness in several forehead and eye-area muscles.[2]
